answer: Shrinking the trigger lowers the latency floor but raises overhead. Each micro-batch cycle pays a fixed planning and offset-commit cost of about 1 second on a typical cluster, so a 100 ms trigger spends almost all its time on overhead and does not deliver near real-time. Below about 1 second the micro-batch model stops paying. Its latency floor is the trigger plus the run, roughly 1 s to minutes. A record-at-a-time engine processes each event as it arrives, with a 10 to 100 ms floor, but it needs a separate API, often a separate cluster, and a second runtime to operate.
